title: Review: Linear equations
description: Questions on the ideas in this chapter, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: What does it mean to solve an equation?
options: Find one value of the unknown that makes it true
Find every value of the unknown that makes it true, and know there are no others
Rewrite it so that the unknown is on the left
Show that both sides are equal for every value of the unknown
questions.explanation: A solution makes the equation true, and solving means finding **all** solutions (:ref{#solution}). Checking that one value works doesn't rule out others.

questions.question: When are two equations called equivalent?
options: When they have exactly the same solutions
When they have at least one solution in common
When they look the same after expanding brackets
When they have the same right-hand side
questions.explanation: Equivalent equations have exactly the same solutions (:ref{#equivalent}). Sharing one solution isn't enough: $$x^2 = 4$$ and $$x = 2$$ share a solution but aren't equivalent.

questions.question: Why is multiplying both sides of an equation by $$0$$ not a safe step?
options: It changes the left side but not the right
It is safe; only dividing by $$0$$ is a problem
It always produces an equation with no solution
It can't be undone, so it can let in false solutions
questions.explanation: Multiplying by $$0$$ turns any equation into $$0 = 0$$, which every number satisfies. A step is safe when it can be undone, and multiplying by $$c$$ can be undone only when $$c \neq 0$$ (:ref{#safe-steps}).

questions.question: Multiplying both sides of $$x = 3$$ by $$x - 1$$ gives $$x(x - 1) = 3(x - 1)$$. What has happened?
options: Nothing: the equations are equivalent
The solution $$x = 3$$ has been lost
A false solution, $$x = 1$$, has been added, because $$x - 1$$ is zero there
The new equation has no solutions
questions.explanation: At $$x = 1$$ both sides of the new equation are $$0$$, so $$x = 1$$ solves it but not $$x = 3$$. Multiplying by an expression is only safe where it isn't zero (:ref{#safe-steps}).

questions.question: Why can squaring both sides of an equation add solutions?
options: Because squaring makes every number positive
Because a number and its opposite have the same square, so the step can't be undone
Because squaring is not allowed in algebra
It can't; squaring always gives an equivalent equation
questions.explanation: Squaring $$x = 3$$ gives $$x^2 = 9$$, which $$x = -3$$ also solves. Since $$3$$ and $$-3$$ square to the same thing, the step can't be undone, so answers must be checked in the original equation (:ref{#safe-steps}).

questions.question: How many solutions does $$ax = c$$ have when $$a = 0$$ and $$c \neq 0$$?
options: None
Exactly one
Infinitely many
It depends on whether $$c$$ is positive
questions.explanation: The left side is $$0 \cdot x = 0$$ for every $$x$$, which never equals $$c \neq 0$$ (:ref{#one-unknown}).

questions.question: While solving a linear equation in $$x$$, the $$x$$ disappears and you are left with $$5 = 5$$. What does that tell you?
options: The equation has no solution
The only solution is $$x = 5$$
You must have made a mistake
Every number is a solution
questions.explanation: The equation has become $$0 \cdot x = 0$$, which every number solves (:ref{#one-unknown}). A false line like $$5 = 7$$ would mean no solution instead.

questions.question: For which numbers $$a$$ does $$ax = c$$ have exactly one solution, whatever $$c$$ is?
options: Only $$a = 1$$
Every positive $$a$$
Every $$a \neq 0$$
Every $$a$$ that divides $$c$$
questions.explanation: When $$a \neq 0$$, $$a$$ has an inverse, and multiplying by it gives the single solution $$x = \frac{c}{a}$$ (:ref{#one-unknown}).

questions.question: How many solutions does a single equation like $$x + y = 5$$ have?
options: None
Infinitely many
Exactly two
Exactly one
questions.explanation: Any $$x$$ can be chosen, and then $$y = 5 - x$$ is forced, so there are infinitely many pairs (:ref{#linear-two}).

questions.question: What is a solution of a system of equations?
options: Values that make every equation true at the same time
Values that make at least one of the equations true
A solution of the first equation
The equation you get by adding all the equations
questions.explanation: A system's equations must hold simultaneously, so a solution makes **every** one of them true (:ref{#system}).

questions.question: Why may you add two equations of a system together?
options: Because adding equations always gives a shorter equation
You may only subtract equations, not add them
Because addition is commutative
Because if both are true for some values, the two left sides are equal to the two right sides, so their sums are equal too
questions.explanation: For values that solve the system, each left side equals its right side, so the sums agree. Combined with the fact that the step can be undone, this gives :ref{#combining}.

questions.question: Replacing equation (2) by (2) plus $$k$$ times (1) gives an equivalent system. Which fact makes the step reversible?
options: $$k$$ must be positive
$$k$$ must be a whole number
Equation (1) is kept, so subtracting $$k$$ times (1) recovers (2)
Both equations must have the same right-hand side
questions.explanation: Because (1) is still in the system, the new equation minus $$k$$ times (1) gives back (2). That is why no solutions are gained or lost (:ref{#combining}). It works for any number $$k$$.

questions.question: Elimination turns a system into $$x = 3$$, $$y = 2$$. Why does that prove $$(3, 2)$$ is the **only** solution of the original system?
options: Because elimination always finds exactly one answer
Because every step gave an equivalent system, so the original has exactly the same solutions as the last one
Because it was checked in one of the equations
It doesn't; there could be other solutions
questions.explanation: Each step of elimination replaces the system by an equivalent one (:ref{#combining}), so the original system has exactly the solutions of the final one, whose only solution is $$(3, 2)$$.

questions.question: After matching, the coefficients of $$y$$ are $$6$$ and $$-6$$. What do you do next?
options: Add the equations
Subtract the equations
Multiply the equations
Divide one equation by the other
questions.explanation: Opposite coefficients cancel when the equations are **added**; equal ones cancel when they are subtracted (:ref{#elimination}).

questions.question: Does the solution depend on which unknown you eliminate first?
options: Yes, eliminating $$x$$ first gives a different answer from eliminating $$y$$
Only when the system has no solution
Only when the coefficients are fractions
No: both routes give equivalent systems, so they reach the same solution
questions.explanation: Every elimination step gives an equivalent system (:ref{#combining}), so whichever unknown goes first, the solutions are the same. Choose the one that keeps the numbers small.

questions.question: After back-substituting into equation (1), why should you check the answer in equation (2)?
options: Checking is never needed if elimination was used
Because (2) is always the harder equation
Back-substitution makes the pair fit equation (1) by construction, so a slip earlier on only shows up in (2)
To find the value of the second unknown
questions.explanation: Back-substitution forces the pair to satisfy the equation you used, so a slip earlier on only shows up in the **other** equation (:ref{#elimination}).

questions.question: Why is it fine to multiply one equation of a system by $$6$$ and another by $$12$$ to clear fractions?
options: Because the multipliers are both even
Because multiplying an equation by a non-zero number doesn't change its solutions
Because both equations must be multiplied by the same number
It isn't; it changes the solution
questions.explanation: Each equation can be multiplied by its own non-zero number without changing its solutions (:ref{#safe-steps}), so the system's solutions don't change either (:ref{#combining}).

questions.question: Substituting $$y = 2x - 3$$ into $$4x + 3y = 11$$, which is right?
questions.explanation: The whole expression replaces $$y$$, so it goes in brackets and the $$3$$ multiplies all of it (:ref{#substitution}).

questions.question: What happens if you substitute $$y = 2x - 3$$ back into the equation it came from?
options: You get the value of $$x$$
You get the value of $$y$$
You get a contradiction
You get something always true, which tells you nothing
questions.explanation: The equation becomes $$2x - 3 = 2x - 3$$, true for every $$x$$. The expression must go into the **other** equation (:ref{#substitution}).

questions.question: Why does replacing $$y$$ by $$E$$ in the other equation, while keeping $$y = E$$, give an equivalent system?
options: Because $$E$$ has no $$y$$ in it
Because substitution is a kind of elimination
Because whenever $$y = E$$ holds, $$y$$ and $$E$$ are the same number, so swapping one for the other can't change whether an equation is true
Because the other equation is linear
questions.explanation: Both systems contain $$y = E$$. For values where that holds, putting $$E$$ in place of $$y$$ leaves both sides of the other equation unchanged (:ref{#substitution-works}).

questions.question: Which method can solve $$y = x + 1$$ together with $$xy = 6$$?
options: Only elimination
Only substitution
Both work equally well
Neither
questions.explanation: Substitution gives $$x(x + 1) = 6$$, an equation in $$x$$ alone. Elimination relies on matching coefficients of linear terms, and $$xy$$ has nothing to cancel against (:ref{#substitution}).

questions.question: When is substitution usually the shorter method?
options: When an unknown is already on its own, or has coefficient $$1$$ or $$-1$$
When all the coefficients are large
When the system has three equations
Never; elimination is always shorter
questions.explanation: If one equation already says $$y = \ldots$$, or rearranges without fractions, substitution is direct (:ref{#substitution}). With awkward coefficients elimination is usually tidier.

questions.question: Elimination leaves the line $$0 = 2$$. What does that mean?
options: The system has infinitely many solutions
You must divide by zero
The solution is $$x = 0$$, $$y = 2$$
The system has no solution
questions.explanation: Every step gave an equivalent system, and no values make $$0 = 2$$ true, so the original system has no solution: it is inconsistent (:ref{#consistent}).

questions.question: Elimination leaves the line $$0 = 0$$. What does that mean?
options: The system has no solution
The only solution is $$(0, 0)$$
One equation said nothing new, and there are infinitely many solutions
The system has exactly one solution
questions.explanation: $$0 = 0$$ is true for all values, so it puts no condition on the unknowns. One equation was a multiple of the other, and the solutions are those of a single equation, of which there are infinitely many (:ref{#determinant-zero}).

questions.question: What is an inconsistent system?
options: One with infinitely many solutions
One with no solution
One whose equations have different numbers of unknowns
One with fractions in it
questions.explanation: A system is consistent if it has at least one solution, and inconsistent if it has none (:ref{#consistent}).

questions.question: What is the determinant of the system $$ax + by = u$$, $$cx + dy = v$$?
options: $$ad - bc$$
$$ab - cd$$
$$ac - bd$$
$$uv - ad$$
questions.explanation: It is the product down one diagonal of the coefficients minus the product down the other: $$ad - bc$$ (:ref{#determinant}).

questions.question: If the determinant of a two-equation system is not zero, how many solutions are there?
options: None
It depends on the right-hand sides
Infinitely many
Exactly one
questions.explanation: A non-zero determinant guarantees exactly one solution, whatever the right-hand sides are (:ref{#determinant-test}).

questions.question: If the determinant is zero, what can the number of solutions be?
options: Only none
Exactly one
None or infinitely many
Exactly two
questions.explanation: With a zero determinant there is never exactly one solution: there are none or infinitely many, depending on the right-hand sides (:ref{#determinant-zero}).

questions.question: In the proof of the formula for the solution, why isn't it enough to derive it by elimination; why must it also be checked?
options: Because elimination only works for whole numbers
Because the elimination used multiplications by $$a$$, $$b$$, $$c$$, $$d$$, which might be zero, so those steps weren't known to be reversible
Because the formula might divide by zero
It is enough; the check is optional
questions.explanation: Deriving it showed that any solution must be that pair. Since some multipliers could be zero, the steps might not be reversible, so the proof checks directly that the pair is a solution (:ref{#determinant-test}).

questions.question: Can a system of two linear equations in two unknowns have exactly two solutions?
options: No: it has exactly one, none or infinitely many
Yes, if the right-hand sides are equal
Yes, if the determinant is zero
Only when the equations are the same
questions.explanation: A non-zero determinant gives exactly one (:ref{#determinant-test}); a zero one gives none or infinitely many (:ref{#determinant-zero}). Indeed, two solutions would give a whole line of them.

questions.question: When does $$ax + by = 0$$, $$cx + dy = 0$$ have a solution other than $$(0, 0)$$?
options: Always
Never
Exactly when $$ad - bc \neq 0$$
Exactly when $$ad - bc = 0$$
questions.explanation: $$(0, 0)$$ is always a solution. A non-zero determinant makes it the only one, and a zero determinant gives infinitely many (:ref{#zero-right-side}).

questions.question: The solutions of a system are written $$(3 - 2t, t)$$ for every number $$t$$. What does the $$t$$ do?
options: It is a third unknown to be solved for
It must equal $$0$$
It is a free choice: each value of $$t$$ gives one of the infinitely many solutions
It is the determinant
questions.explanation: Choosing $$y = t$$ freely forces $$x = 3 - 2t$$, and different values of $$t$$ give different solutions. This is how infinitely many solutions are written down exactly. The proof of :ref{#determinant-zero} builds solutions in the same way, by adding multiples of a fixed pair to one solution.

questions.question: In the proof that a zero determinant gives infinitely many solutions (once there is one), why is a pair $$(p, q)$$ with $$ap + bq = 0$$ and $$cp + dq = 0$$ useful?
options: It is the solution of the system
Adding any multiple $$t(p, q)$$ to a solution leaves both left-hand sides unchanged, giving more solutions
It shows the determinant is zero
It shows the system is inconsistent
questions.explanation: If $$(x_0, y_0)$$ is a solution, then $$a(x_0 + tp) + b(y_0 + tq) = u + t \cdot 0 = u$$, and likewise for the second equation, so every $$t$$ gives a solution (:ref{#determinant-zero}).

questions.question: What is the graph of an equation in $$x$$ and $$y$$?
options: The set of all points whose coordinates solve the equation
A picture of the left-hand side
The point where it crosses the $$y$$-axis
Its slope
questions.explanation: The graph is all the points $$(x, y)$$ that are solutions (:ref{#graph}). For a linear equation it is a straight line (:ref{#line}).

questions.question: What does the solution of a system of two linear equations look like on a graph?
options: The origin
The point where each line crosses the $$x$$-axis
The steeper of the two lines
The point where the lines cross
questions.explanation: A solution lies on both lines, so it is a point where they cross (:ref{#graph}).

questions.question: Two different lines are parallel. What does that say about the system?
options: It has exactly one solution
It has infinitely many solutions
It has no solution
It has two solutions
questions.explanation: Parallel lines never meet, so no point lies on both: the system is inconsistent. This matches a zero determinant with contradicting equations (:ref{#parallel-test}).

questions.question: Two equations draw the same line. How many solutions does the system have?
options: None
Infinitely many
Exactly two
Exactly one
questions.explanation: Every point on the line lies on both graphs, so every one is a solution (:ref{#graph}).

questions.question: What is the slope of $$3x + 2y = 6$$?
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives $$y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 3$$, so the slope is $$-\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{3}{2}$$ (:ref{#slope}).

questions.question: Which equation $$ax + by = c$$ gives a vertical line with no slope?
options: One with $$a = 0$$
One with $$a = b$$
One with $$c = 0$$
One with $$b = 0$$
questions.explanation: When $$b = 0$$ the equation is $$ax = c$$, which fixes $$x$$ and lets $$y$$ be anything: a vertical line. The slope $$-\frac{a}{b}$$ isn't defined (:ref{#slope}).

questions.question: What does a zero determinant mean for the two lines?
options: They cross exactly once
They cross at the origin
They point the same way: parallel or the same line
They are at right angles
questions.explanation: For non-vertical lines, $$ad - bc = 0$$ exactly when the slopes are equal (:ref{#parallel-test}), so the lines are parallel or coincide.

questions.question: Why solve a system with algebra rather than reading the crossing point off a drawing?
options: Drawings always give the wrong answer
Drawings are only approximate, while elimination gives the exact point
Algebra is faster to draw
Lines can't be drawn accurately for whole numbers
questions.explanation: A sketch shows roughly where lines meet, but a crossing point like $$(\frac{31}{38}, -\frac{8}{19})$$ can only be found exactly by algebra (:ref{#elimination}). The picture is for understanding and checking.

questions.question: When solving three equations, why must both new equations be free of the same unknown?
options: So that they form two equations in the same two unknowns
Because the third unknown is always zero
To make the numbers smaller
It doesn't matter which unknowns they are free of
questions.explanation: If one new equation lacks $$z$$ and the other lacks $$y$$, all three unknowns are still involved. Removing the same one twice leaves a two-unknown system (:ref{#three-method}).

questions.question: Why must the two eliminations in step 2 use different pairs of equations?
options: They don't; any two combinations will do
Because each equation may only be used once
Because it makes the numbers smaller
Using one pair twice only repeats the information in those two equations, and loses the third
questions.explanation: Two combinations of the same pair carry only what those two equations say. The third equation has to be used, or its condition is lost (:ref{#three-method}).

questions.question: How many equations are usually needed to pin down three unknowns?
options: One
Two
Three
Six
questions.explanation: One equation leaves two of the unknowns free to choose. Each further equation that says something new pins down one more, so three unknowns usually need three equations (:ref{#linear-three}).

questions.question: Solving three equations in three unknowns, you reach $$0 = 0$$. What has happened?
options: The system has no solution
One of the equations was a combination of the others, so it said nothing new
The solution is $$(0, 0, 0)$$
You must start again with a different unknown
questions.explanation: An always-true line means one equation followed from the others. The system then has the solutions of the remaining two, and may have infinitely many (:ref{#combining}).

questions.question: After clearing fractions and solving, where should you check the answer?
options: In the original equations
In the cleared equations
In the two-unknown system
Checking isn't needed
questions.explanation: A slip while clearing fractions wouldn't show up in the cleared equations, so the check belongs in the original ones (:ref{#three-method}).
